children: The Federal Reserve Board will consider final revisions to its stress testing framework in coming weeks, Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Friday.

The changes are designed to "improve transparency and public accountability, strengthen the reliability and accuracy of the models, and reduce the volatility of the capital requirements flowing from the annual stress test results," she said in a speech at an event in London.

Furthermore, she expects the Fed board to finalize reforms to risk-based capital requirements for large and small banks as well as improvements to the global systematically important bank (G-SIB) surcharge.
"In totality, these reforms create a durable and lasting framework to produce capital requirements that are rational, robust, aligned with risk, and transparent," she said.

She also discussed the results of the central bank's analysis of Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse. Fed staff supervising banks should have known about Silicon Valley Bank's vulnerabilities as early as March 2022, about a year before the bank failed. Another factor contributing to the supervisory inaction was a "long-standing culture of risk aversion," she said.

The Fed will consider two final rules for revising the annual bank stress tests. The first final rule would require publishing detailed information on the stress test models and on the scenario design process, a move to make the Fed more accountable to the public. The second final rule would reduce the volatility of the stress capital buffer requirement by averaging the results of a bank's two most recent annual stress tests. The changes will also move the effective date of the new SCB to the following Jan. 1 from Oct. 1. "The change aligns compliance to calendar year and provides additional time to implement the resulting capital requirements," she said.

Bowman said she'll also recommend a third proposal that will revise the 2027 test models to allow for public feedback. "The proposal will seek public comment on a revised model for noninterest income, which is the fee and trading revenue that banks earn from activities including wealth management, investment banking, and market making," she said. "This model would better capture business diversity across firms and would replace the existing noninterest income model for the 2027 stress test."

The stress tests should serve as a valuable tool in supervising banks, she said. "In theory, stress tests should identify unique firm vulnerabilities to material financial and nonfinancial risks. They should also provide insight into stressful scenarios that would cause those risks to materialize."
The tests should identify a firm's vulnerability and allow them to address them before material financial and nonfinancial risks emerge, she said.

"Our approach will achieve this increased transparency and public accountability while making capital-related stress testing more accurate, effective, predictable, and fair," Bowman said in her conclusion.

title: Fed's Bowman proposes bank stress testing changes to increase transparency, reduce SCB volatility
